$comment: Branching troubleshooting scenarios for the Study Bot. Each node has text, optional evidence, and choices {label, next, score, feedback}; an end node has end {rootCause, lesson}.

scenarios.title: Pipeline gets 403 from ACR, intermittently
scenarios.intro: Your Azure Pipelines build pushes images to Azure Container Registry. About one run in five fails at docker push with "403 Forbidden". Re-running usually works.

n1.text: What do you look at first?

choices.label: The exact error and which agent ran the failing jobs
choices.feedback: Good: intermittent failures that vary by run often vary by agent.

choices.label: Give the service principal Owner on the registry
choices.feedback: That grants far more than needed and does not explain why it works most of the time.

choices.label: Recreate the service connection
choices.feedback: It might be needed later, but first find what differs between passing and failing runs.

n1x.text: Owner did not help - the next run still failed. Back to the evidence.

choices.label: Look at the error and the agents

n2.text: The failing runs all ran on the self-hosted pool 'build-linux'; passing runs used Microsoft-hosted agents. The error says: denied: client with IP '20.1.2.3' is not allowed access.
n2.evidence: ACR firewall: public network access 'Selected networks', allowed: the Microsoft-hosted agents' service tag ranges.

choices.label: The registry firewall blocks the self-hosted agents' outbound IP
choices.feedback: Exactly - it is network, not RBAC: 403 with 'client with IP ... is not allowed'.

choices.label: The AcrPush role is missing
choices.feedback: RBAC is fine - the same identity pushes successfully from hosted agents.

choices.label: Docker credentials expire mid-build
choices.feedback: The message names an IP, which points at network rules.

n3w.text: Look again at the message: it names a client IP. What controls which IPs may reach the registry?

choices.label: The registry's network rules

n3.text: How do you fix it properly?

choices.label: Give the self-hosted agents a private endpoint path to ACR (Premium SKU) and disable public access
choices.feedback: Best: no public exposure, agents reach ACR over the VNet.

choices.label: Add the agents' NAT gateway public IP to the ACR firewall
choices.feedback: Works and is quick; a private endpoint is the stronger long-term fix.

choices.label: Allow all networks
choices.feedback: That removes the protection entirely.

end.rootCause: The ACR firewall only allowed the Microsoft-hosted agents' ranges; jobs on the self-hosted pool came from a different public IP and got 403 from the registry's network rules.
end.lesson: A 403 from a PaaS service can be network access, not RBAC. Read the message - 'client with IP ... is not allowed' - and compare what differs between passing and failing runs.

scenarios.title: Pods in CrashLoopBackOff after a deploy
scenarios.intro: After deploying version 2.4 of the orders API to AKS, all new pods go into CrashLoopBackOff. Version 2.3 ran fine.

choices.label: kubectl describe pod and kubectl logs --previous
choices.feedback: Yes - describe shows events and the exit reason; --previous shows the crashed container's logs.

choices.label: Scale the deployment to 10 replicas
choices.feedback: More copies of a crashing container still crash.

choices.label: Delete the namespace and redeploy
choices.feedback: Destructive, and you lose the evidence.

n2.text: describe shows: Last State: Terminated, Reason: Error, Exit Code: 1. logs --previous: 'Unhandled exception: Configuration key ConnectionStrings:Orders not found'.
n2.evidence: The 2.4 Helm values reference a secret 'orders-db' with key 'connection'; the cluster secret has key 'connectionString'.

choices.label: The app cannot find its configuration - check the secret and env mapping
choices.feedback: Right - exit 1 with a config error is an application start-up failure.

choices.label: It is an OOMKilled problem - raise memory limits
choices.feedback: OOM shows Reason: OOMKilled and exit code 137, not exit 1 with a config error.

choices.label: The node is unhealthy
choices.feedback: All new pods fail on every node, and old pods run - it follows the version.

n3w.text: Re-read the logs: they name a missing configuration key.

choices.label: Check the config mapping
Roll back to 2.3 now, then fix the key mapping and add a config check to the pipeline
choices.feedback: Restore service first, then fix forward with a guard.

choices.label: Edit the secret in production by hand to match
choices.feedback: Fixes it, but untracked manual changes drift; fix in source and roll out.

choices.label: Wait for Kubernetes to retry
choices.feedback: CrashLoopBackOff only backs off further; it will not fix configuration.

end.rootCause: Version 2.4 expected the secret key 'connection' but the cluster secret used 'connectionString', so the app exited at start-up with code 1.
end.lesson: CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom. Exit code and previous logs tell you why: 1 = app error, 137 = OOMKilled/SIGKILL, 143 = SIGTERM.

scenarios.title: 502s right after a slot swap
scenarios.intro: You swapped the staging slot of an App Service web app into production. For about three minutes users got 502 errors, then everything recovered.

n1.text: What is the most likely class of cause?

choices.label: The new code was not warmed up when it started taking traffic
choices.feedback: Yes - a short burst of errors right after a swap is the classic cold start.

choices.label: A DNS change during the swap
choices.feedback: Swaps do not change DNS; traffic is switched inside the platform.

choices.label: The App Service plan is too small
choices.feedback: Possible, but the errors lasted minutes and stopped - more like warm-up.

n2.text: Logs show the app takes 90 seconds to load caches at start-up. The staging slot had been stopped before the swap. There is no applicationInitialization in web.config and no health check path set.

choices.label: Keep staging running and warm it before swapping, using applicationInitialization or a custom warm-up path
choices.feedback: Swap waits for warm-up when you configure it.

choices.label: Use swap with preview
choices.feedback: Good: it applies production settings to staging and lets you verify before completing.

choices.label: Restart production after every swap
choices.feedback: That causes another cold start.

n3.text: What else prevents users seeing errors?

choices.label: Configure Health check so unhealthy instances are taken out of rotation
choices.feedback: Health check stops routing to instances that are not ready.

choices.label: Use deployment slot sticky settings for connection strings
choices.feedback: Important for correctness, but not the cause here.

choices.label: Disable the swap and deploy straight to production
choices.feedback: That makes downtime worse, not better.

end.rootCause: Production received traffic on a cold instance: staging was stopped and there was no warm-up configuration, so the app spent 90 seconds loading caches while returning 502s.
end.lesson: Swaps are near-zero-downtime only when the source slot is running and warmed: applicationInitialization (or WEBSITE_SWAP_WARMUP_PING_PATH), swap with preview, and Health check.

scenarios.title: VM loses access to storage after a private endpoint
scenarios.intro: A storage account was given a private endpoint and public network access was disabled. Now a VM in a spoke VNet gets '403 This request is not authorized to perform this operation'.

choices.label: Resolve the storage account name from the VM (nslookup)
choices.feedback: Yes - a private endpoint only helps if the name resolves to its private IP.

choices.label: Check the VM identity's RBAC role on the account
choices.feedback: Worth knowing, but nothing about RBAC changed - the network did.

choices.label: Re-enable public network access
choices.feedback: That undoes the security change instead of fixing it.

n2.text: nslookup mystore.blob.core.windows.net returns a public IP via mystore.privatelink.blob.core.windows.net.
n2.evidence: The privatelink.blob.core.windows.net zone exists in the hub, linked to the hub VNet only. The spoke uses Azure-provided DNS.

choices.label: The private DNS zone is not linked to the spoke VNet
choices.feedback: Right - the spoke's resolver cannot see the zone, so it gets the public answer.

choices.label: The private endpoint is in the wrong subnet
choices.feedback: Peered VNets can reach it wherever it is; the name resolves publicly, so DNS is the problem.

choices.label: TLS certificate mismatch
choices.feedback: The error is 403 from the public endpoint, not a TLS failure.

choices.label: Link the privatelink zone to the spoke (or make the spoke use the hub's DNS resolver)
choices.feedback: Then the CNAME chain resolves to the private IP.

choices.label: Add a hosts file entry on the VM
choices.feedback: Works on one VM but does not scale and breaks if the IP changes.

choices.label: Create a second privatelink zone in the spoke
choices.feedback: Duplicate zones cause inconsistent resolution across the estate.

end.rootCause: The spoke VNet could not see the privatelink.blob zone, so the storage name resolved to the public endpoint - which was disabled - giving 403.
end.lesson: With private endpoints, 'it is always DNS': check what the name resolves to from the client, and which zones its resolver can see.

scenarios.title: Terraform pipeline stuck on a state lock
scenarios.intro: Your Terraform apply stage fails with 'Error acquiring the state lock: state blob is already locked'. The last run was cancelled halfway through.

n1.text: What does the lock tell you?

choices.label: Another run - or the cancelled one - still holds the lease on the state blob
choices.feedback: Yes - the azurerm backend uses a blob lease as the lock.

choices.label: The state file is corrupted
choices.feedback: A lock error is about concurrency, not corruption.

choices.label: The storage account key expired
choices.feedback: That would fail authentication, not lock acquisition.

n2.text: No other pipeline run is active. The error output shows Lock Info with ID a1b2-..., Who: build-agent-7, Created: 2 hours ago - the cancelled run.

choices.label: Confirm nothing is running, then terraform force-unlock <lock-id>
choices.feedback: Correct, and only after confirming no run is active.

choices.label: Break the blob lease in the portal
choices.feedback: Also works for the azurerm backend; force-unlock is the Terraform way.

choices.label: Delete the state file and re-import everything
choices.feedback: Never - the state is your source of truth.

end.rootCause: The cancelled run never released its lease on the state blob, so later runs could not acquire the lock.
end.lesson: Locks protect state from concurrent writes. Release a stale lock only after confirming nothing else is running, and avoid hard-cancelling apply stages.

scenarios.title: The Azure bill doubled overnight
scenarios.intro: Finance reports yesterday's Azure spend was twice the usual daily amount. Nobody admits to deploying anything.

choices.label: Cost analysis grouped by service and resource for yesterday vs the previous week
choices.feedback: Find which resource changed before guessing why.

choices.label: Delete the most expensive resources
choices.feedback: You might delete production.

choices.label: Ask every team in a channel
choices.feedback: People help, but data first is faster.

n2.text: Cost analysis: the increase is all 'Virtual Machines - D16s v5' in resource group rg-batch, 40 instances, created yesterday at 01:00.
n2.evidence: Activity log: a VM scale set's capacity changed from 2 to 40 at 01:00 by the autoscale engine; the custom metric it scales on was stuck at 100%.

choices.label: An autoscale rule scaled out on a broken metric and never scaled in
choices.feedback: Right - the activity log shows the scale-out and its trigger.

choices.label: Someone deployed 40 VMs by hand
choices.feedback: The activity log says the autoscale engine changed capacity.

choices.label: Reserved instance expired
choices.feedback: That changes price per hour, not the number of instances.

choices.label: Fix the metric, set a sensible maximum instance count, add a scale-in rule, and a budget alert with action group
choices.feedback: Fix cause, cap blast radius, detect earlier.

choices.label: Disable autoscale permanently
choices.feedback: Stops the spike but loses elasticity.

choices.label: Just add a budget alert
choices.feedback: Detection is good, but the cause and the cap remain.

end.rootCause: A VM scale set autoscaled from 2 to 40 instances on a custom metric stuck at 100%, with a high maximum and no effective scale-in.
end.lesson: For cost spikes: cost analysis by resource, then the activity log for who/what changed it. Protect with max instance counts, budgets and anomaly alerts.

scenarios.title: ImagePullBackOff after ACR went private
scenarios.intro: You moved Azure Container Registry behind a private endpoint and disabled public access. Existing pods on AKS keep running, but every new pod sticks in ImagePullBackOff.

choices.label: kubectl describe pod - the pull error in the events
choices.feedback: The events carry the kubelet's real error.

choices.label: Restart the nodes
choices.feedback: Old pods run from cached images; a reboot would break them too.

choices.label: Re-assign AcrPull to the kubelet identity
choices.feedback: It is already there - nothing changes, but you still need the real error.

n1x.text: Two nodes rebooted and now their pods cannot start either. Get the actual error.

choices.label: kubectl describe pod

n2.text: Event: failed to pull image "myacr.azurecr.io/shop:1.4": dial tcp 20.50.1.9:443: i/o timeout.
n2.evidence: From a debug pod: nslookup myacr.azurecr.io → 20.50.1.9 (public), not the endpoint's 10.1.4.5.

choices.label: DNS gives the registry's public IP, which is now blocked
choices.feedback: Right: a private endpoint only helps if the name resolves to its private IP.

choices.label: The AcrPull role is missing
A NetworkPolicy blocks egress

n2w.text: Egress is not blocked: the timeout is to a public address. Why would the registry resolve to one?

choices.label: Look at private DNS

wrong-rbac.text: You re-check RBAC and close the ticket as a permissions issue.

end.rootCause: You blamed RBAC, but an authorisation failure is a 401/403 - this was a network timeout to a public IP.
end.lesson: Read the error class first: timeouts are network or DNS, 401/403 are identity.

n3.evidence: Private DNS zone privatelink.azurecr.io has A records for myacr and myacr.westeurope.data, but is linked only to the hub VNet. The AKS spoke VNet uses Azure-provided DNS.

choices.label: Link the privatelink.azurecr.io zone to the AKS VNet (or forward to the hub's resolver)
choices.feedback: That makes the nodes resolve the private IP.

choices.label: Add a hosts-file entry on every node

wrong-hosts.text: You add hosts entries and pulls work - until the node pool scales.

end.rootCause: A hosts-file hack hides the missing DNS zone link; new nodes and IP changes break it again.
end.lesson: Fix name resolution where it lives: zone links or resolver forwarding.

end.rootCause: The registry's private DNS zone was not linked to the AKS VNet, so nodes resolved the public endpoint, which disabled public access blocks.
end.lesson: With private endpoints the DNS zone link (or resolver forwarding) is part of the deployment - and ACR's data endpoint (<registry>.<region>.data.azurecr.io) needs a record too.

scenarios.title: Application Gateway 502 after a certificate renewal
scenarios.intro: The backend team renewed the TLS certificate on the web VMs. Since then Application Gateway v2 returns 502 Bad Gateway for every request.

choices.label: Application Gateway Backend health
choices.feedback: It says exactly why the gateway marks backends unhealthy.

choices.label: Restart the backend VMs
Scale out the gateway
choices.feedback: A 502 on every request is not capacity.

n1x.text: Still 502 everywhere. What does the gateway think of its backends?

choices.label: Open Backend health

n2.evidence: Message: "The Common Name (CN) of the backend server certificate does not match the host header...". New certificate CN: app.contoso.com. Backend setting: connects by IP with no host name override.

choices.label: The new certificate's name does not match the host name the gateway uses - set it in the backend setting and probe
choices.feedback: Yes: v2 validates the backend certificate against the host name it sends.

choices.label: Upload the new certificate to the HTTPS listener
Switch the backend to plain HTTP

n2w.text: The listener certificate is the client-facing one and it is fine. The failure is gateway → backend. Read the health message again.

choices.label: Back to Backend health

wrong-http.text: You switch the backend to HTTP and the 502s stop.

end.rootCause: You removed end-to-end TLS instead of fixing the host-name mismatch.
end.lesson: Keep end-to-end TLS; make the host name in the backend setting and probe match the certificate.

end.text: Backends turn Healthy and traffic flows.

end.rootCause: The renewed backend certificate's CN/SAN did not match the host name Application Gateway used (it connected by IP), so v2 rejected it.
end.lesson: For end-to-end TLS on v2, set the host name in backend settings (or pick it from the backend target), use the same host name in custom probes, and use a well-known CA or upload the trusted root.

scenarios.title: SQL timeouts at peak after a release
scenarios.intro: Since Tuesday's release the API on App Service throws SQL timeouts during the evening peak. CPU on the App Service plan sits at 35%.

choices.label: Compare Azure SQL metrics (CPU, waits) with the times of the timeouts
choices.feedback: The app tier is idle - look where the time goes.

choices.label: Scale the App Service plan up
choices.feedback: App CPU is 35%; the wait is elsewhere.

choices.label: Raise the command timeout to 5 minutes
choices.feedback: That hides the symptom and holds connections longer.

n1x.text: No change: timeouts continue at peak. What about the database?

choices.label: Check Azure SQL metrics

n2.text: Azure SQL CPU hits 100% from 19:00 to 21:00 since Tuesday; before, it peaked at 45%.
n2.evidence: Query Performance Insight: GetOrdersByCustomer uses 70% of CPU. Query Store shows its plan changed on Tuesday to a clustered index scan after the release added a Status filter.

choices.label: A query regression from the release: the new filter has no supporting index
choices.feedback: Yes - one query, a new plan, a scan.

choices.label: The database tier is too small - scale it up
Network latency between App Service and SQL

n2w.text: Latency is flat; CPU is not. What is using it?

choices.label: Back to the CPU evidence

wrong-scale.text: You scale the database up two tiers and the timeouts stop - for now.

end.rootCause: Scaling up bought headroom, but the regressed query still scans; cost went up and the problem returns as data grows.
end.lesson: Find the query first. Scale only when the workload, not a regression, needs it.

n3.text: How do you fix it tonight and for good?

choices.label: Force the last good plan in Query Store now; ship the missing index in a migration
choices.feedback: Safe immediately, and fixed properly.

choices.label: Rebuild every index

n3w.text: The rebuild runs for an hour; CPU is still pinned and the query still scans.

choices.label: Back to the options

end.text: CPU drops to 40% at peak and the timeouts stop.

end.rootCause: The release added a filter without a supporting index; the plan changed to a scan and saturated Azure SQL CPU at peak.
end.lesson: Check database metrics before scaling the app tier. Query Store shows plan regressions and can force a known-good plan while the index ships.

scenarios.title: Key Vault references fail after an RBAC switch
scenarios.intro: The security team switched Key Vault kv-shop to the Azure RBAC permission model. Now App Service settings that use Key Vault references fail and the app will not start.

choices.label: The Key Vault reference status on the app's environment variables
choices.feedback: It shows why each reference failed to resolve.

choices.label: Rotate the secret
Restart the app
choices.feedback: It fails the same way.

n1x.text: Nothing changes. What does App Service say about the references?

choices.label: Check the reference status

n2.text: Reference status: AccessToKeyVaultDenied. Identity: the system-assigned managed identity of app-shop.
n2.evidence: Access policies still list app-shop with Get/List on secrets. Permission model: Azure role-based access control. Role assignments on kv-shop: Key Vault Administrator for the security group only.

choices.label: With the RBAC model access policies are ignored - the identity needs a data role
choices.feedback: Exactly.

choices.label: The vault firewall blocks App Service
Recreate the access policy

n2w.text: Networking did not change, and the status says access denied, not blocked by firewall. What did change?

choices.label: The permission model

wrong-policy.text: You recreate the access policy and restart. Same error.

end.rootCause: Access policies are ignored once a vault uses Azure RBAC, so recreating them changes nothing.
end.lesson: Know which permission model a vault uses before changing access.

n3.text: What do you grant, and where?

choices.label: Key Vault Secrets User for app-shop's identity on kv-shop (or just the secrets it needs)
choices.feedback: Least privilege at the right scope.

choices.label: Key Vault Administrator on the subscription

n3w.text: Security rejects the change: far beyond least privilege.

choices.label: Choose again

end.text: References resolve and the app starts.

end.rootCause: Switching to the Azure RBAC permission model made the vault ignore its access policies; the app's managed identity had no data-plane role.
end.lesson: Before switching models, turn access policies into role assignments (e.g. Key Vault Secrets User at vault or secret scope). New assignments can take a few minutes to apply.
